# Draft (AI-assisted) — new paper by the same author

In recent years, the resilience of seagrass meadows has garnered significant attention as a crucial component of coastal ecosystem health. In this study, we embarked on a comprehensive investigation to shed light on the intricate relationship between turbidity and seagrass density across a diverse array of estuarine environments, which is a topic of paramount importance given the multifaceted pressures facing coastal zones in the contemporary era.

We surveyed 64 meadow sites across two estuaries, measuring shoot density in five 0.25-m² quadrats per site. Our findings reveal that shoot density was markedly lower at sites where mean turbidity exceeded 12 NTU, thereby underscoring the pivotal role that light availability plays in shaping meadow structure. Furthermore, it is worth noting that this pattern was observed in both estuaries. Additionally, sites closer to river mouths exhibited higher turbidity.

It should be emphasized that there are some limitations. The study only sampled during the dry season, which may potentially limit the generalizability of the findings to the wet season, when turbidity is likely to be higher.
